case_info.scenario: A 46-year-old woman was referred for a second opinion regarding hydroxychloroquine retinal toxicity. Her medical history included systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), diabetes type 1, nonalcoholic steatohepatosis, mild congenital hearing loss, and anemia. SLE was managed with azathioprine and belimumab, and she had been taking hydroxychloroquine, 400 mg, daily for 5 years before the medication was recently stopped due to concern for retinal toxicity. Review of systems was notable for imbalance, cognitive decline, major depression, and recent onset of suspected seizures. Snellen visual acuity was 20/30 OD and 20/20 OS and intraocular pressures were normal. Results of slitlamp examination of the anterior segment were unremarkable, with clear corneas, quiet anterior chambers, and clear lenses bilaterally. Fundus examination revealed bilateral discrete perifoveal circular areas of atrophy. The optic discs and fundus were otherwise unremarkable. Fundus autofluorescence and optical coherence tomography (OCT) revealed perifoveal hypoautofluorescence corresponding with complete retinal pigment epithelium and outer retinal atrophy on OCT (Figureand insert). Automated 10-2 visual field testing revealed dense paracentral ring scotomata bilaterally.

case_info.explanation: Mitochondrial encephalomyopathy, lactic acidosis, and strokelike episodes This patient’s presentation was atypical for hydroxychloroquine retinal toxicity. Her pattern of perifoveal atrophy was more consistent with inherited mitochondrial disease, and ocular findings were discussed with neurology, medical genetics, and rheumatology teams in the context of progressive neurologic symptoms, which prompted genetic evaluation. Genetic testing revealed a pathogenicMT-TL1m.3243A>G sequence variation (heteroplasmy 23%), the most common variation causing mitochondrial encephalomyopathy, lactic acidosis, and strokelike episodes (MELAS). MELAS, while relatively rare in the general population, is one of the more common mitochondrial myopathies, with a population-dependent prevalence between 0.18 and 236 per 100 000 individuals.1Similar to other mitochondrial diseases, MELAS is either maternally inherited or may arise from de novo mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) sequence variations, most commonly A to G transition at mtDNA position 3243.2,3Age at onset is variable but usually manifests before age 40 years with any combination of seizures, strokelike episodes, progressive cognitive deterioration, myopathy, and variable involvement of other organs.1,4,5Disease severity is impacted by heteroplasmy, the proportion of pathogenic mtDNA, and potentially by coexisting nuclear DNA sequence variations.6Potential associations include diabetes, sensorineural hearing loss, and cardiac disorders. The most common clinical presentation of retinopathy associated withMT-TL1m.3243A>G sequence variations is circumferential perifoveal atrophy, initially discontinuous, as in this patient, which may coalesce over time.4Fundus autofluorescence imaging typically demonstrates hypoautofluorescence in areas of advanced chorioretinal atrophy with surrounding speckled hyperautofluorescence. Other possible ocular manifestations include ophthalmoplegia, nystagmus, cataract, and optic nerve atrophy.7Visual acuity is variable but often good at presentation.4 Diagnosis of MELAS may be confirmed with genetic testing in the context of relevant clinical findings (including encephalopathy and strokelike episodes), laboratory clues (including elevated lactate levels in serum and cerebrospinal fluid [CSF]), and muscle biopsy evaluating for ragged red fibers. Comprehensive systemic evaluation is imperative for identification and management of associated conditions. Management of MELAS is mainly supportive and also critically involves avoiding medications that can cause mitochondrial toxicity (eg, valproic acid) or lactic acidosis (eg, metformin).1Multiple studies have supported a role for arginine supplementation in the management and prevention of strokelike episodes,8as well as for other vitamins and supplements including coenzyme Q10, creatine, and carnitine as part of a “mitochondrial cocktail” for patients with mitochondrial cytopathies.9 Option A is incorrect. While discontinuing hydroxychloroquine may be reasonable in the context of this patient’s maculopathy,10further evaluation is warranted to make the appropriate diagnosis and to ensure appropriate monitoring, identification of associated systemic manifestations, genetic counseling, and potential evaluation of family members. Options B and C are incorrect. While there is outer retinal and retinal pigment epithelium atrophy on OCT, the patient is relatively young and lacks other findings consistent with age-related macular degeneration. The patient’s systemic manifestations of MELAS were managed by her multidisciplinary health care team. Her evaluation revealed elevated lactic acid in the serum and CSF. Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain showed diffuse parenchymal volume loss for her age, with disproportionate cerebellum involvement and scattered chronic lacunar infarcts in the basal ganglia and left thalamus. She was prescribed arginine, carnitine, and coenzyme Q10, as well as vitamins A, D, E, K, and a vitamin B complex. She continued insulin treatment for her diabetes, lactulose, rifaximin, and sodium benzoate for cirrhosis-associated encephalopathy, as well as antiepileptic medication.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.

case_info.explanation: Mitochondrial encephalomyopathy, lactic acidosis, and strokelike episodes This patient’s presentation was atypical for hydroxychloroquine retinal toxicity. Her pattern of perifoveal atrophy was more consistent with inherited mitochondrial disease, and ocular findings were discussed with neurology, medical genetics, and rheumatology teams in the context of progressive neurologic symptoms, which prompted genetic evaluation. Genetic testing revealed a pathogenicMT-TL1m.3243A>G sequence variation (heteroplasmy 23%), the most common variation causing mitochondrial encephalomyopathy, lactic acidosis, and strokelike episodes (MELAS). MELAS, while relatively rare in the general population, is one of the more common mitochondrial myopathies, with a population-dependent prevalence between 0.18 and 236 per 100 000 individuals.1Similar to other mitochondrial diseases, MELAS is either maternally inherited or may arise from de novo mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) sequence variations, most commonly A to G transition at mtDNA position 3243.2,3Age at onset is variable but usually manifests before age 40 years with any combination of seizures, strokelike episodes, progressive cognitive deterioration, myopathy, and variable involvement of other organs.1,4,5Disease severity is impacted by heteroplasmy, the proportion of pathogenic mtDNA, and potentially by coexisting nuclear DNA sequence variations.6Potential associations include diabetes, sensorineural hearing loss, and cardiac disorders. The most common clinical presentation of retinopathy associated withMT-TL1m.3243A>G sequence variations is circumferential perifoveal atrophy, initially discontinuous, as in this patient, which may coalesce over time.4Fundus autofluorescence imaging typically demonstrates hypoautofluorescence in areas of advanced chorioretinal atrophy with surrounding speckled hyperautofluorescence. Other possible ocular manifestations include ophthalmoplegia, nystagmus, cataract, and optic nerve atrophy.7Visual acuity is variable but often good at presentation.4 Diagnosis of MELAS may be confirmed with genetic testing in the context of relevant clinical findings (including encephalopathy and strokelike episodes), laboratory clues (including elevated lactate levels in serum and cerebrospinal fluid [CSF]), and muscle biopsy evaluating for ragged red fibers. Comprehensive systemic evaluation is imperative for identification and management of associated conditions. Management of MELAS is mainly supportive and also critically involves avoiding medications that can cause mitochondrial toxicity (eg, valproic acid) or lactic acidosis (eg, metformin).1Multiple studies have supported a role for arginine supplementation in the management and prevention of strokelike episodes,8as well as for other vitamins and supplements including coenzyme Q10, creatine, and carnitine as part of a “mitochondrial cocktail” for patients with mitochondrial cytopathies.9 Option A is incorrect. While discontinuing hydroxychloroquine may be reasonable in the context of this patient’s maculopathy,10further evaluation is warranted to make the appropriate diagnosis and to ensure appropriate monitoring, identification of associated systemic manifestations, genetic counseling, and potential evaluation of family members. Options B and C are incorrect. While there is outer retinal and retinal pigment epithelium atrophy on OCT, the patient is relatively young and lacks other findings consistent with age-related macular degeneration. The patient’s systemic manifestations of MELAS were managed by her multidisciplinary health care team. Her evaluation revealed elevated lactic acid in the serum and CSF. Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain showed diffuse parenchymal volume loss for her age, with disproportionate cerebellum involvement and scattered chronic lacunar infarcts in the basal ganglia and left thalamus. She was prescribed arginine, carnitine, and coenzyme Q10, as well as vitamins A, D, E, K, and a vitamin B complex. She continued insulin treatment for her diabetes, lactulose, rifaximin, and sodium benzoate for cirrhosis-associated encephalopathy, as well as antiepileptic medication.

case_info.explanation: Mitochondrial encephalomyopathy, lactic acidosis, and strokelike episodes This patient’s presentation was atypical for hydroxychloroquine retinal toxicity. Her pattern of perifoveal atrophy was more consistent with inherited mitochondrial disease, and ocular findings were discussed with neurology, medical genetics, and rheumatology teams in the context of progressive neurologic symptoms, which prompted genetic evaluation. Genetic testing revealed a pathogenicMT-TL1m.3243A>G sequence variation (heteroplasmy 23%), the most common variation causing mitochondrial encephalomyopathy, lactic acidosis, and strokelike episodes (MELAS). MELAS, while relatively rare in the general population, is one of the more common mitochondrial myopathies, with a population-dependent prevalence between 0.18 and 236 per 100 000 individuals.1Similar to other mitochondrial diseases, MELAS is either maternally inherited or may arise from de novo mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) sequence variations, most commonly A to G transition at mtDNA position 3243.2,3Age at onset is variable but usually manifests before age 40 years with any combination of seizures, strokelike episodes, progressive cognitive deterioration, myopathy, and variable involvement of other organs.1,4,5Disease severity is impacted by heteroplasmy, the proportion of pathogenic mtDNA, and potentially by coexisting nuclear DNA sequence variations.6Potential associations include diabetes, sensorineural hearing loss, and cardiac disorders. The most common clinical presentation of retinopathy associated withMT-TL1m.3243A>G sequence variations is circumferential perifoveal atrophy, initially discontinuous, as in this patient, which may coalesce over time.4Fundus autofluorescence imaging typically demonstrates hypoautofluorescence in areas of advanced chorioretinal atrophy with surrounding speckled hyperautofluorescence. Other possible ocular manifestations include ophthalmoplegia, nystagmus, cataract, and optic nerve atrophy.7Visual acuity is variable but often good at presentation.4 Diagnosis of MELAS may be confirmed with genetic testing in the context of relevant clinical findings (including encephalopathy and strokelike episodes), laboratory clues (including elevated lactate levels in serum and cerebrospinal fluid [CSF]), and muscle biopsy evaluating for ragged red fibers. Comprehensive systemic evaluation is imperative for identification and management of associated conditions. Management of MELAS is mainly supportive and also critically involves avoiding medications that can cause mitochondrial toxicity (eg, valproic acid) or lactic acidosis (eg, metformin).1Multiple studies have supported a role for arginine supplementation in the management and prevention of strokelike episodes,8as well as for other vitamins and supplements including coenzyme Q10, creatine, and carnitine as part of a “mitochondrial cocktail” for patients with mitochondrial cytopathies.9 Option A is incorrect. While discontinuing hydroxychloroquine may be reasonable in the context of this patient’s maculopathy,10further evaluation is warranted to make the appropriate diagnosis and to ensure appropriate monitoring, identification of associated systemic manifestations, genetic counseling, and potential evaluation of family members. Options B and C are incorrect. While there is outer retinal and retinal pigment epithelium atrophy on OCT, the patient is relatively young and lacks other findings consistent with age-related macular degeneration. The patient’s systemic manifestations of MELAS were managed by her multidisciplinary health care team. Her evaluation revealed elevated lactic acid in the serum and CSF. Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain showed diffuse parenchymal volume loss for her age, with disproportionate cerebellum involvement and scattered chronic lacunar infarcts in the basal ganglia and left thalamus. She was prescribed arginine, carnitine, and coenzyme Q10, as well as vitamins A, D, E, K, and a vitamin B complex. She continued insulin treatment for her diabetes, lactulose, rifaximin, and sodium benzoate for cirrhosis-associated encephalopathy, as well as antiepileptic medication.

case_info.explanation: Mitochondrial encephalomyopathy, lactic acidosis, and strokelike episodes This patient’s presentation was atypical for hydroxychloroquine retinal toxicity. Her pattern of perifoveal atrophy was more consistent with inherited mitochondrial disease, and ocular findings were discussed with neurology, medical genetics, and rheumatology teams in the context of progressive neurologic symptoms, which prompted genetic evaluation. Genetic testing revealed a pathogenicMT-TL1m.3243A>G sequence variation (heteroplasmy 23%), the most common variation causing mitochondrial encephalomyopathy, lactic acidosis, and strokelike episodes (MELAS). MELAS, while relatively rare in the general population, is one of the more common mitochondrial myopathies, with a population-dependent prevalence between 0.18 and 236 per 100 000 individuals.1Similar to other mitochondrial diseases, MELAS is either maternally inherited or may arise from de novo mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) sequence variations, most commonly A to G transition at mtDNA position 3243.2,3Age at onset is variable but usually manifests before age 40 years with any combination of seizures, strokelike episodes, progressive cognitive deterioration, myopathy, and variable involvement of other organs.1,4,5Disease severity is impacted by heteroplasmy, the proportion of pathogenic mtDNA, and potentially by coexisting nuclear DNA sequence variations.6Potential associations include diabetes, sensorineural hearing loss, and cardiac disorders. The most common clinical presentation of retinopathy associated withMT-TL1m.3243A>G sequence variations is circumferential perifoveal atrophy, initially discontinuous, as in this patient, which may coalesce over time.4Fundus autofluorescence imaging typically demonstrates hypoautofluorescence in areas of advanced chorioretinal atrophy with surrounding speckled hyperautofluorescence. Other possible ocular manifestations include ophthalmoplegia, nystagmus, cataract, and optic nerve atrophy.7Visual acuity is variable but often good at presentation.4 Diagnosis of MELAS may be confirmed with genetic testing in the context of relevant clinical findings (including encephalopathy and strokelike episodes), laboratory clues (including elevated lactate levels in serum and cerebrospinal fluid [CSF]), and muscle biopsy evaluating for ragged red fibers. Comprehensive systemic evaluation is imperative for identification and management of associated conditions. Management of MELAS is mainly supportive and also critically involves avoiding medications that can cause mitochondrial toxicity (eg, valproic acid) or lactic acidosis (eg, metformin).1Multiple studies have supported a role for arginine supplementation in the management and prevention of strokelike episodes,8as well as for other vitamins and supplements including coenzyme Q10, creatine, and carnitine as part of a “mitochondrial cocktail” for patients with mitochondrial cytopathies.9 Option A is incorrect. While discontinuing hydroxychloroquine may be reasonable in the context of this patient’s maculopathy,10further evaluation is warranted to make the appropriate diagnosis and to ensure appropriate monitoring, identification of associated systemic manifestations, genetic counseling, and potential evaluation of family members. Options B and C are incorrect. While there is outer retinal and retinal pigment epithelium atrophy on OCT, the patient is relatively young and lacks other findings consistent with age-related macular degeneration. The patient’s systemic manifestations of MELAS were managed by her multidisciplinary health care team. Her evaluation revealed elevated lactic acid in the serum and CSF. Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain showed diffuse parenchymal volume loss for her age, with disproportionate cerebellum involvement and scattered chronic lacunar infarcts in the basal ganglia and left thalamus. She was prescribed arginine, carnitine, and coenzyme Q10, as well as vitamins A, D, E, K, and a vitamin B complex. She continued insulin treatment for her diabetes, lactulose, rifaximin, and sodium benzoate for cirrhosis-associated encephalopathy, as well as antiepileptic medication.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

case_info.explanation: Mitochondrial encephalomyopathy, lactic acidosis, and strokelike episodes This patient’s presentation was atypical for hydroxychloroquine retinal toxicity. Her pattern of perifoveal atrophy was more consistent with inherited mitochondrial disease, and ocular findings were discussed with neurology, medical genetics, and rheumatology teams in the context of progressive neurologic symptoms, which prompted genetic evaluation. Genetic testing revealed a pathogenicMT-TL1m.3243A>G sequence variation (heteroplasmy 23%), the most common variation causing mitochondrial encephalomyopathy, lactic acidosis, and strokelike episodes (MELAS). MELAS, while relatively rare in the general population, is one of the more common mitochondrial myopathies, with a population-dependent prevalence between 0.18 and 236 per 100 000 individuals.1Similar to other mitochondrial diseases, MELAS is either maternally inherited or may arise from de novo mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) sequence variations, most commonly A to G transition at mtDNA position 3243.2,3Age at onset is variable but usually manifests before age 40 years with any combination of seizures, strokelike episodes, progressive cognitive deterioration, myopathy, and variable involvement of other organs.1,4,5Disease severity is impacted by heteroplasmy, the proportion of pathogenic mtDNA, and potentially by coexisting nuclear DNA sequence variations.6Potential associations include diabetes, sensorineural hearing loss, and cardiac disorders. The most common clinical presentation of retinopathy associated withMT-TL1m.3243A>G sequence variations is circumferential perifoveal atrophy, initially discontinuous, as in this patient, which may coalesce over time.4Fundus autofluorescence imaging typically demonstrates hypoautofluorescence in areas of advanced chorioretinal atrophy with surrounding speckled hyperautofluorescence. Other possible ocular manifestations include ophthalmoplegia, nystagmus, cataract, and optic nerve atrophy.7Visual acuity is variable but often good at presentation.4 Diagnosis of MELAS may be confirmed with genetic testing in the context of relevant clinical findings (including encephalopathy and strokelike episodes), laboratory clues (including elevated lactate levels in serum and cerebrospinal fluid [CSF]), and muscle biopsy evaluating for ragged red fibers. Comprehensive systemic evaluation is imperative for identification and management of associated conditions. Management of MELAS is mainly supportive and also critically involves avoiding medications that can cause mitochondrial toxicity (eg, valproic acid) or lactic acidosis (eg, metformin).1Multiple studies have supported a role for arginine supplementation in the management and prevention of strokelike episodes,8as well as for other vitamins and supplements including coenzyme Q10, creatine, and carnitine as part of a “mitochondrial cocktail” for patients with mitochondrial cytopathies.9 Option A is incorrect. While discontinuing hydroxychloroquine may be reasonable in the context of this patient’s maculopathy,10further evaluation is warranted to make the appropriate diagnosis and to ensure appropriate monitoring, identification of associated systemic manifestations, genetic counseling, and potential evaluation of family members. Options B and C are incorrect. While there is outer retinal and retinal pigment epithelium atrophy on OCT, the patient is relatively young and lacks other findings consistent with age-related macular degeneration. The patient’s systemic manifestations of MELAS were managed by her multidisciplinary health care team. Her evaluation revealed elevated lactic acid in the serum and CSF. Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain showed diffuse parenchymal volume loss for her age, with disproportionate cerebellum involvement and scattered chronic lacunar infarcts in the basal ganglia and left thalamus. She was prescribed arginine, carnitine, and coenzyme Q10, as well as vitamins A, D, E, K, and a vitamin B complex. She continued insulin treatment for her diabetes, lactulose, rifaximin, and sodium benzoate for cirrhosis-associated encephalopathy, as well as antiepileptic medication.

   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.

   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.

   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and

       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.

       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's

case_info.explanation: Mitochondrial encephalomyopathy, lactic acidosis, and strokelike episodes This patient’s presentation was atypical for hydroxychloroquine retinal toxicity. Her pattern of perifoveal atrophy was more consistent with inherited mitochondrial disease, and ocular findings were discussed with neurology, medical genetics, and rheumatology teams in the context of progressive neurologic symptoms, which prompted genetic evaluation. Genetic testing revealed a pathogenicMT-TL1m.3243A>G sequence variation (heteroplasmy 23%), the most common variation causing mitochondrial encephalomyopathy, lactic acidosis, and strokelike episodes (MELAS). MELAS, while relatively rare in the general population, is one of the more common mitochondrial myopathies, with a population-dependent prevalence between 0.18 and 236 per 100 000 individuals.1Similar to other mitochondrial diseases, MELAS is either maternally inherited or may arise from de novo mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) sequence variations, most commonly A to G transition at mtDNA position 3243.2,3Age at onset is variable but usually manifests before age 40 years with any combination of seizures, strokelike episodes, progressive cognitive deterioration, myopathy, and variable involvement of other organs.1,4,5Disease severity is impacted by heteroplasmy, the proportion of pathogenic mtDNA, and potentially by coexisting nuclear DNA sequence variations.6Potential associations include diabetes, sensorineural hearing loss, and cardiac disorders. The most common clinical presentation of retinopathy associated withMT-TL1m.3243A>G sequence variations is circumferential perifoveal atrophy, initially discontinuous, as in this patient, which may coalesce over time.4Fundus autofluorescence imaging typically demonstrates hypoautofluorescence in areas of advanced chorioretinal atrophy with surrounding speckled hyperautofluorescence. Other possible ocular manifestations include ophthalmoplegia, nystagmus, cataract, and optic nerve atrophy.7Visual acuity is variable but often good at presentation.4 Diagnosis of MELAS may be confirmed with genetic testing in the context of relevant clinical findings (including encephalopathy and strokelike episodes), laboratory clues (including elevated lactate levels in serum and cerebrospinal fluid [CSF]), and muscle biopsy evaluating for ragged red fibers. Comprehensive systemic evaluation is imperative for identification and management of associated conditions. Management of MELAS is mainly supportive and also critically involves avoiding medications that can cause mitochondrial toxicity (eg, valproic acid) or lactic acidosis (eg, metformin).1Multiple studies have supported a role for arginine supplementation in the management and prevention of strokelike episodes,8as well as for other vitamins and supplements including coenzyme Q10, creatine, and carnitine as part of a “mitochondrial cocktail” for patients with mitochondrial cytopathies.9 Option A is incorrect. While discontinuing hydroxychloroquine may be reasonable in the context of this patient’s maculopathy,10further evaluation is warranted to make the appropriate diagnosis and to ensure appropriate monitoring, identification of associated systemic manifestations, genetic counseling, and potential evaluation of family members. Options B and C are incorrect. While there is outer retinal and retinal pigment epithelium atrophy on OCT, the patient is relatively young and lacks other findings consistent with age-related macular degeneration. The patient’s systemic manifestations of MELAS were managed by her multidisciplinary health care team. Her evaluation revealed elevated lactic acid in the serum and CSF. Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain showed diffuse parenchymal volume loss for her age, with disproportionate cerebellum involvement and scattered chronic lacunar infarcts in the basal ganglia and left thalamus. She was prescribed arginine, carnitine, and coenzyme Q10, as well as vitamins A, D, E, K, and a vitamin B complex. She continued insulin treatment for her diabetes, lactulose, rifaximin, and sodium benzoate for cirrhosis-associated encephalopathy, as well as antiepileptic medication.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

Her medical history included systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), diabetes type 1, nonalcoholic steatohepatosis, mild congenital hearing loss, and anemia. Snellen visual acuity was 20/30 OD and 20/20 OS and intraocular pressures were normal. Results of slitlamp examination of the anterior segment were unremarkable, with clear corneas, quiet anterior chambers, and clear lenses bilaterally. Fundus examination revealed bilateral discrete perifoveal circular areas of atrophy. The optic discs and fundus were otherwise unremarkable. Fundus autofluorescence and optical coherence tomography (OCT) revealed perifoveal hypoautofluorescence corresponding with complete retinal pigment epithelium and outer retinal atrophy on OCT (Figureand insert). Automated 10-2 visual field testing revealed dense paracentral ring scotomata bilaterally.

case_info.explanation: Mitochondrial encephalomyopathy, lactic acidosis, and strokelike episodes This patient’s presentation was atypical for hydroxychloroquine retinal toxicity. Her pattern of perifoveal atrophy was more consistent with inherited mitochondrial disease, and ocular findings were discussed with neurology, medical genetics, and rheumatology teams in the context of progressive neurologic symptoms, which prompted genetic evaluation. Genetic testing revealed a pathogenicMT-TL1m.3243A>G sequence variation (heteroplasmy 23%), the most common variation causing mitochondrial encephalomyopathy, lactic acidosis, and strokelike episodes (MELAS). MELAS, while relatively rare in the general population, is one of the more common mitochondrial myopathies, with a population-dependent prevalence between 0.18 and 236 per 100 000 individuals.1Similar to other mitochondrial diseases, MELAS is either maternally inherited or may arise from de novo mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) sequence variations, most commonly A to G transition at mtDNA position 3243.2,3Age at onset is variable but usually manifests before age 40 years with any combination of seizures, strokelike episodes, progressive cognitive deterioration, myopathy, and variable involvement of other organs.1,4,5Disease severity is impacted by heteroplasmy, the proportion of pathogenic mtDNA, and potentially by coexisting nuclear DNA sequence variations.6Potential associations include diabetes, sensorineural hearing loss, and cardiac disorders. The most common clinical presentation of retinopathy associated withMT-TL1m.3243A>G sequence variations is circumferential perifoveal atrophy, initially discontinuous, as in this patient, which may coalesce over time.4Fundus autofluorescence imaging typically demonstrates hypoautofluorescence in areas of advanced chorioretinal atrophy with surrounding speckled hyperautofluorescence. Other possible ocular manifestations include ophthalmoplegia, nystagmus, cataract, and optic nerve atrophy.7Visual acuity is variable but often good at presentation.4 Diagnosis of MELAS may be confirmed with genetic testing in the context of relevant clinical findings (including encephalopathy and strokelike episodes), laboratory clues (including elevated lactate levels in serum and cerebrospinal fluid [CSF]), and muscle biopsy evaluating for ragged red fibers. Comprehensive systemic evaluation is imperative for identification and management of associated conditions. Management of MELAS is mainly supportive and also critically involves avoiding medications that can cause mitochondrial toxicity (eg, valproic acid) or lactic acidosis (eg, metformin).1Multiple studies have supported a role for arginine supplementation in the management and prevention of strokelike episodes,8as well as for other vitamins and supplements including coenzyme Q10, creatine, and carnitine as part of a “mitochondrial cocktail” for patients with mitochondrial cytopathies.9 Option A is incorrect. While discontinuing hydroxychloroquine may be reasonable in the context of this patient’s maculopathy,10further evaluation is warranted to make the appropriate diagnosis and to ensure appropriate monitoring, identification of associated systemic manifestations, genetic counseling, and potential evaluation of family members. Options B and C are incorrect. While there is outer retinal and retinal pigment epithelium atrophy on OCT, the patient is relatively young and lacks other findings consistent with age-related macular degeneration. The patient’s systemic manifestations of MELAS were managed by her multidisciplinary health care team. Her evaluation revealed elevated lactic acid in the serum and CSF. Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain showed diffuse parenchymal volume loss for her age, with disproportionate cerebellum involvement and scattered chronic lacunar infarcts in the basal ganglia and left thalamus. She was prescribed arginine, carnitine, and coenzyme Q10, as well as vitamins A, D, E, K, and a vitamin B complex. She continued insulin treatment for her diabetes, lactulose, rifaximin, and sodium benzoate for cirrhosis-associated encephalopathy, as well as antiepileptic medication.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

1. Mental Demand

   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."

       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."

   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to

       the case?"

case_info.explanation: Mitochondrial encephalomyopathy, lactic acidosis, and strokelike episodes This patient’s presentation was atypical for hydroxychloroquine retinal toxicity. Her pattern of perifoveal atrophy was more consistent with inherited mitochondrial disease, and ocular findings were discussed with neurology, medical genetics, and rheumatology teams in the context of progressive neurologic symptoms, which prompted genetic evaluation. Genetic testing revealed a pathogenicMT-TL1m.3243A>G sequence variation (heteroplasmy 23%), the most common variation causing mitochondrial encephalomyopathy, lactic acidosis, and strokelike episodes (MELAS). MELAS, while relatively rare in the general population, is one of the more common mitochondrial myopathies, with a population-dependent prevalence between 0.18 and 236 per 100 000 individuals.1Similar to other mitochondrial diseases, MELAS is either maternally inherited or may arise from de novo mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) sequence variations, most commonly A to G transition at mtDNA position 3243.2,3Age at onset is variable but usually manifests before age 40 years with any combination of seizures, strokelike episodes, progressive cognitive deterioration, myopathy, and variable involvement of other organs.1,4,5Disease severity is impacted by heteroplasmy, the proportion of pathogenic mtDNA, and potentially by coexisting nuclear DNA sequence variations.6Potential associations include diabetes, sensorineural hearing loss, and cardiac disorders. The most common clinical presentation of retinopathy associated withMT-TL1m.3243A>G sequence variations is circumferential perifoveal atrophy, initially discontinuous, as in this patient, which may coalesce over time.4Fundus autofluorescence imaging typically demonstrates hypoautofluorescence in areas of advanced chorioretinal atrophy with surrounding speckled hyperautofluorescence. Other possible ocular manifestations include ophthalmoplegia, nystagmus, cataract, and optic nerve atrophy.7Visual acuity is variable but often good at presentation.4 Diagnosis of MELAS may be confirmed with genetic testing in the context of relevant clinical findings (including encephalopathy and strokelike episodes), laboratory clues (including elevated lactate levels in serum and cerebrospinal fluid [CSF]), and muscle biopsy evaluating for ragged red fibers. Comprehensive systemic evaluation is imperative for identification and management of associated conditions. Management of MELAS is mainly supportive and also critically involves avoiding medications that can cause mitochondrial toxicity (eg, valproic acid) or lactic acidosis (eg, metformin).1Multiple studies have supported a role for arginine supplementation in the management and prevention of strokelike episodes,8as well as for other vitamins and supplements including coenzyme Q10, creatine, and carnitine as part of a “mitochondrial cocktail” for patients with mitochondrial cytopathies.9 Option A is incorrect. While discontinuing hydroxychloroquine may be reasonable in the context of this patient’s maculopathy,10further evaluation is warranted to make the appropriate diagnosis and to ensure appropriate monitoring, identification of associated systemic manifestations, genetic counseling, and potential evaluation of family members. Options B and C are incorrect. While there is outer retinal and retinal pigment epithelium atrophy on OCT, the patient is relatively young and lacks other findings consistent with age-related macular degeneration. The patient’s systemic manifestations of MELAS were managed by her multidisciplinary health care team. Her evaluation revealed elevated lactic acid in the serum and CSF. Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain showed diffuse parenchymal volume loss for her age, with disproportionate cerebellum involvement and scattered chronic lacunar infarcts in the basal ganglia and left thalamus. She was prescribed arginine, carnitine, and coenzyme Q10, as well as vitamins A, D, E, K, and a vitamin B complex. She continued insulin treatment for her diabetes, lactulose, rifaximin, and sodium benzoate for cirrhosis-associated encephalopathy, as well as antiepileptic medication.

A 46-year-old woman was referred for a second opinion regarding hydroxychloroquine retinal toxicity. Her medical history included systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), diabetes type 1, nonalcoholic steatohepatosis, mild congenital hearing loss, and anemia. SLE was managed with azathioprine and belimumab, and she had been taking hydroxychloroquine, 400 mg, daily for 5 years before the medication was recently stopped due to concern for retinal toxicity. Review of systems was notable for imbalance, cognitive decline, major depression, and recent onset of suspected seizures. Snellen visual acuity was 20/30 OD and 20/20 OS and intraocular pressures were normal. Results of slitlamp examination of the anterior segment were unremarkable, with clear corneas, quiet anterior chambers, and clear lenses bilaterally. Fundus examination revealed bilateral discrete perifoveal circular areas of atrophy. The optic discs and fundus were otherwise unremarkable. Fundus autofluorescence and optical coherence tomography (OCT) revealed perifoveal hypoautofluorescence corresponding with complete retinal pigment epithelium and outer retinal atrophy on OCT (Figureand insert). Automated 10-2 visual field testing revealed dense paracentral ring scotomata bilaterally.
